summary: Acyclovir is a nucleoside-analogue antiviral selective for herpes viruses (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV). It is used to treat shingles, genital herpes, and chickenpox. It requires viral thymidine kinase for activation, giving it a good safety profile, but it needs renal dose adjustment and adequate hydration to avoid crystalluria and nephrotoxicity.
indications: Treatment of initial and recurrent genital herpes

dosage.n: For 5 days; start within 24 h of rash

dosage.d: 20 mg/kg (max 800 mg) per dose 4 times daily

admin: May be taken with or without food
Ensure adequate hydration to reduce risk of renal precipitation
Begin therapy at the earliest sign or symptom (prodrome) for best efficacy
moa: A guanosine analogue that is phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase to acyclovir monophosphate, then to the active triphosphate by cellular kinases. Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase and incorporates into viral DNA, causing chain termination. Selective for infected cells.
preg: Generally considered acceptable for use in pregnancy when indicated; pregnancy registry data have not shown an increased risk of birth defects. Use if benefit justifies potential risk.
lact: Excreted into breast milk but considered compatible with breastfeeding; infant exposure is low relative to therapeutic pediatric doses.
renal: Requires dose reduction based on creatinine clearance. Reduce dose/frequency in renal impairment; ensure hydration to prevent crystalluria and acute kidney injury. For oral zoster: CrCl <10 reduce to 800 mg every 12 hours.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is generally needed.

moderate: Probenecid (decreases renal clearance, raises acyclovir levels)
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate BUN and serum creatinine

serious: Neurotoxicity (confusion, hallucinations, tremor) - especially renal impairment
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura/hemolytic uremic syndrome (immunocompromised, high dose)

monitoring: Renal function (creatinine, BUN), especially with IV or in renal impairment
Neurologic symptoms in elderly or renal impairment
CBC in immunocompromised patients on prolonged therapy
counsel: Start treatment as early as possible when symptoms begin
Complete the entire course even if symptoms improve
Acyclovir reduces symptoms and transmission risk but does not cure herpes
Report confusion, reduced urination, or unusual fatigue
pk: Antiviral activity begins shortly after absorption; clinical benefit greatest if started early
Plasma peak ~1.5-2 hours after oral dose
Short - requires frequent (4-5 times daily) oral dosing
Store at 15-25 C; protect from moisture and light
pearls: Oral bioavailability is low (~15-30%), necessitating frequent dosing
Valacyclovir (prodrug) gives higher bioavailability and less frequent dosing for many indications
Adequate hydration is key to preventing nephrotoxicity
Selective for virus-infected cells via dependence on viral thymidine kinase
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered, then continue the regular schedule. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one - do not double up.
overdose: Overdose (often from accumulation in renal impairment) may cause agitation, confusion, hallucinations, seizures, and renal failure. Management is supportive with hydration; hemodialysis effectively removes acyclovir and may be used in severe cases.
